name: D1.1 Ethics and the three pillars (CIA)

paragraphes: Your neighbor goes on vacation. He gives you his house keys so you can water his plants.
You could walk in whenever you want and look around. Nobody is watching you. Still, you don't do it.
What stops you is your honesty. A cybersecurity professional also holds many keys. Their honesty is written in a code of ethics: rules of conduct they promise to follow.

decouverte.titre: It is like the rules of a sports club
decouverte.comme: A player signs the club's rules: respect the referee, do not cheat, protect the club's image. The rules do not say what to do every second of the match. The player has to think.
decouverte.enVrai: The (ISC)2 code of ethics works the same way. (ISC)2 is the organization that awards the CISSP. Its code has four main rules, called canons. They guide your judgment without replacing it. A member who knowingly breaks them can lose their certification.

decouverte.question: You are an (ISC)2 member. You see another member break the code of ethics. What should a member do in this case?
options: Nothing: it is not your business
Settle it in secret with them
decouverte.explanation: (ISC)2 asks you to follow the official complaint procedure. Staying silent can be seen as a breach of the code. The other two choices seem kind, but they do not protect the profession.

decouverte.texte: You work at a company. A colleague asks you to read the messages of a person he dislikes. Technically, you have the access. But the code asks you to act honestly and to protect public trust. Being able to do something does not mean you have the right to do it.

decouverte.titre: It is like choosing a plumber
decouverte.comme: You call a plumber. He comes into your home and sees your things. You choose him because his reputation is good. One doubt about him, and you call someone else.
decouverte.enVrai: The preamble says the same: a member must follow the code and also be seen following it. Even a doubt about their conduct can put their place at risk. The people you work for (your employer, your clients) are called principals.

cards.question: Official definition: “(ISC)2 Code of Ethics Preamble”
cards.answer: The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, and be seen to adhere, to the highest ethical standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of certification.
cards.explanation: Two ideas to remember: act well, and be seen to act well.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand, Adhere to, and Promote Professional Ethics”. You need to know it word for word.

cards.question: The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we [[adhere]], and be seen to adhere, to the highest ethical standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of [[certification]].
cards.answer: The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, and be seen to adhere, to the highest ethical standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of certification.
cards.explanation: Two key words: adhere (follow the code) and certification (if you do not follow the code, you lose the certificate).

cards.question: The [[safety and welfare of society]] and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, and [[be seen to adhere]], to the [[highest ethical standards]] of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of certification.
cards.answer: The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, and be seen to adhere, to the highest ethical standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of certification.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the good of society, being seen to follow the code, and very high standards.

cards.question: Write the preamble of the (ISC)2 code of ethics from memory (in English).
cards.answer: The safety and welfare of society and the common good, duty to our principals, and to each other, requires that we adhere, and be seen to adhere, to the highest ethical standards of behavior. Therefore, strict adherence to this Code of Ethics is a condition of certification.
cards.explanation: No need to be perfect on the first try: compare, spot what is missing, try again tomorrow.

cards.question: Official definition: the role of the four canons of the code of ethics
cards.answer: The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics includes four canons that are intended to serve as high-level guidelines to augment, not replace, members' professional judgment.
cards.explanation: The canons are general guideposts: they help you think, they do not think for you.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “(ISC)2 Code of Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics includes [[four canons]] that are intended to serve as [[high-level guidelines]] to [[augment, not replace]], members' professional judgment.
cards.answer: The (ISC)2 Code of Ethics includes four canons that are intended to serve as high-level guidelines to augment, not replace, members' professional judgment.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the number of canons, their role as guides, and the fact that they add to your judgment.

cards.question: Official definition: “Canon I”
cards.answer: Canon I: Protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure.
cards.explanation: Canon I: society comes first. The infrastructure means the networks and services everyone depends on.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. The four canons in order: society, honesty, clients, profession.

cards.question: Canon I: [[Protect society]], the common good, necessary [[public trust and confidence]], and [[the infrastructure]].
cards.answer: Canon I: Protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: protect society, keep the trust of the public, protect the infrastructure.

cards.question: Official definition: “Canon II”
cards.answer: Canon II: Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally.
cards.explanation: Canon II: honesty and the law. Five adverbs, almost all ending in -ly.

cards.question: Canon II: [[Act honorably]], [[honestly]], justly, responsibly, and [[legally]].
cards.answer: Canon II: Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally.
cards.explanation: The first, second and last items of the list: honorably, honestly, legally.

cards.question: Official definition: “Canon III”
cards.answer: Canon III: Provide diligent and competent service to principals.
cards.explanation: Canon III: your work for your employer or your clients must be careful and competent.

cards.question: Canon III: [[Provide diligent]] and [[competent service]] to [[principals]].
cards.answer: Canon III: Provide diligent and competent service to principals.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: diligent work, competent service, and who it is for: the principals.

cards.question: Official definition: “Canon IV”
cards.answer: Canon IV: Advance and protect the profession.
cards.explanation: Canon IV: the profession. Every member helps keep its good name.

cards.question: Canon IV: [[Advance]] and [[protect]] the [[profession]].
cards.answer: Canon IV: Advance and protect the profession.
cards.explanation: Two verbs, one noun: advance, protect, the profession.

cards.question: You see an (ISC)2 member break the code of ethics. What is the right reaction?
options: Wait: it is none of your business
cards.answer: Follow the published complaint procedure
cards.explanation: (ISC)2 asks you to follow the official complaint procedure.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Code of Professional Ethics”. Not doing so can be seen as a failure to respect Canon IV.

cards.question: You are certified. You post a joke saying you break into your school's accounts. You never did it. Why is it still a problem?
options: There is no problem: you did nothing wrong
People may doubt how serious you are, even without a real fault
Only actions count, never the image you give
The code forbids all humor for members
options_why: The preamble asks you to be seen following the code: your image matters too.
On the contrary: even the appearance of a fault can put your place at risk.
The code says nothing about humor: it talks about honesty, service and reputation.
cards.answer: People may doubt how serious you are, even without a real fault
cards.explanation: The manual says that even the perception of a fault can put a member's place at risk.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, explanation of the preamble: members must be visible ethical leaders.

cards.question: Which canon does each behavior belong to?
cards.answer: Canon I: the dangerous system and the city networks. Canon II: the admitted mistake and the law. Canon III: careful work and training. Canon IV: reporting and helping beginners.
cards.explanation: Ask yourself who you are protecting: society, the truth, the client or the profession.

items.text: Refuse to deliver a system that would put the public in danger
Protect the networks that a whole city depends on
Honestly admit a mistake you made
Obey the law even when it slows down your work
Give your client careful and competent work
Train yourself to serve your employer better
Report a member who breaks the code
Help beginners so that the profession stays respected

cards.question: Why does the code of ethics not replace your professional judgment?
cards.answer: The four canons are broad guidelines. No list covers every situation, so you have to think for yourself.
cards.explanation: The canons guide your thinking, they do not replace it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: the canons are meant to augment, not replace, professional judgment (“augment, not replace”).

cards.question: What does an (ISC)2 member risk by knowingly breaking the code?
cards.answer: A review by their peers (peer review) and possible penalties, up to losing their certification.
cards.explanation: The code is not just advice: it has consequences.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand, Adhere to, and Promote Professional Ethics”.

cards.question: A member must follow the code of ethics and also be [[seen|visible]] following it.
cards.answer: A member must follow the code of ethics and also be seen following it.
cards.explanation: This is the idea of the preamble: “be seen to adhere”.

cards.question: Besides the (ISC)2 code, which other code of ethics must you know?
cards.answer: The one your employer or your industry requires of you.
cards.explanation: It does not replace your common sense or your own morals.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Organizational Code of Ethics”. A CISSP must also set an example by following it.

concepts.name: Information security and the CIA Triad

paragraphes: Your school keeps every student's grades in a big register. These grades are information: valuable things to know.
Imagine everything that could go wrong with this register. Protecting information is the mission of information security.
To make sense of it, experts sum up this mission in three pillars, called the CIA Triad.

decouverte.comme: Your diary has a padlock. First problem: a curious person reads it. Second: someone scribbles on your pages. Third: you lose the key and cannot open it.
decouverte.enVrai: The curious reader is a loss of confidentiality. The scribbles are a loss of integrity. The lost key is a loss of availability. You will keep this diary in mind throughout the galaxy.

decouverte.question: On an online shop, a hacker copies the customers' addresses. Another changes the prices to one euro. A third takes the site down on sale day. How many pillars are hit?
decouverte.explanation: Copying addresses hits secrecy. Changing prices hits accuracy. Taking the site down hits access. Each attack targets a different pillar.

decouverte.comme: A tripod stands thanks to its three legs. If even one is missing, the camera falls.
decouverte.enVrai: The CIA Triad has three pillars that work together. The letters stand for three English words. They have nothing to do with the secret service agency of the same name. The image stops there: a tripod has no favorite leg. But in security, one pillar can matter more than another depending on the company.

decouverte.texte: A hospital keeps a file for each patient. Only the patient's care team should read it. A dose of medicine must never be changed by mistake. And the file must open at once in the emergency room. Three needs, three pillars.

cards.question: Official definition: “information security”
cards.answer: Information security refers to the processes and methodologies involved in safeguarding information and underlying systems from inappropriate access, use, modification, or disturbance.
cards.explanation: Remember the verb: safeguarding means protecting.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand and Apply Security Concepts”. You need to know it word for word.

cards.question: Information security refers to the processes and methodologies involved in [[safeguarding]] information and underlying systems from inappropriate access, use, modification, or [[disturbance]].
cards.answer: Information security refers to the processes and methodologies involved in safeguarding information and underlying systems from inappropriate access, use, modification, or disturbance.
cards.explanation: The two key words: safeguarding (protecting) and disturbance.

cards.question: Information security refers to the [[processes and methodologies]] involved in [[safeguarding information]] and underlying systems from [[inappropriate access]], use, modification, or disturbance.
cards.answer: Information security refers to the processes and methodologies involved in safeguarding information and underlying systems from inappropriate access, use, modification, or disturbance.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the methods, protecting information, and inappropriate access.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “information security” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: Information security refers to the processes and methodologies involved in safeguarding information and underlying systems from inappropriate access, use, modification, or disturbance.
cards.explanation: Compare: did you name the four dangers: access, use, modification and disturbance?

cards.question: Official definition: “CIA Triad”
cards.answer: This is most often described by three critical security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Together, these three principles form the pillars of information security known as the CIA Triad.
cards.explanation: Three words, three initials: C, I, A.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. The “This” at the start means information security.

cards.question: This is most often described by three critical security concepts: confidentiality, [[integrity]], and availability. Together, these three principles form the [[pillars]] of information security known as the CIA Triad.
cards.answer: This is most often described by three critical security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Together, these three principles form the pillars of information security known as the CIA Triad.
cards.explanation: Two words to remember: integrity in the middle of the list, and pillars.

cards.question: This is most often described by [[three critical security concepts]]: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Together, these three principles form the [[pillars of information security]] known as the [[CIA Triad]].
cards.answer: This is most often described by three critical security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Together, these three principles form the pillars of information security known as the CIA Triad.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the three concepts, the pillars of security, and the name of the triad.

cards.question: Write the manual's sentence about the “CIA Triad” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: This is most often described by three critical security concepts: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Together, these three principles form the pillars of information security known as the CIA Triad.
cards.explanation: Check that you have the three words, in the right order.

cards.question: A hacker changes the price of an item to one euro on a website. Which pillar is hit?
cards.answer: Integrity
cards.explanation: Nothing was read in secret: some data was changed. Changing data is integrity.

cards.question: In the word CIA, what does the A stand for?
options_why: This word exists in security, but it is not the A of the triad.
This word is close to availability, but it is not the A of the triad.
It is not a pillar of the triad.
cards.answer: Availability
cards.explanation: The A comes from availability: authorized people can reach the data when they need it.

cards.question: Which box does each situation go in?
cards.answer: Confidentiality: the photographed files and the password that was read. Integrity: the changed grades and the typo. Availability: the unreachable shop and the flooded server room.
cards.explanation: Ask yourself: did someone see what they should not, change something, or block access?

items.text: A stranger photographs customer files left on a desk
A student's password is read by a classmate
A hacker changes the grades in a register
A typo turns 100 euros into 1000 euros
The online shop cannot be reached during the sales
A flood destroys the server room

cards.question: Why do we say the three pillars depend on each other?
cards.answer: One pillar alone is not enough. Data that is secret but false, or correct but impossible to open, is useless.
cards.explanation: The three work together to keep information protected.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. The three concepts work together and depend on each other. One type of system may favor one of them.

cards.question: In the emergency room, doctors can no longer open the patients' files. Nobody has read or changed these files. Which pillar is hit?
options_why: Nobody read these files without the right to.
The files were not modified: they are just out of reach.
cards.answer: Availability
cards.explanation: Authorized people cannot reach the data when they need it.

cards.question: What are the three pillars of the CIA Triad?
cards.answer: Confidentiality, integrity and availability.
cards.explanation: One initial per pillar: C, I, A.

cards.question: The [[CIA]] Triad groups confidentiality, [[integrity]] and availability.
cards.answer: The CIA Triad groups confidentiality, integrity and availability.
cards.explanation: The name CIA comes from the three initials: C, I, A.

cards.question: Explain the CIA Triad to a 13-year-old friend, with an example of your choice.
cards.answer: Three ways to protect information. Confidentiality: only the right readers can see it. Integrity: nobody changes it without the right to. Availability: authorized people can open it when they need it.
cards.explanation: A good example is worth more than a definition learned by heart.

paragraphes: You write your secrets in a diary. You put a padlock on it.
One day, someone opens it in secret, reads it, then closes it again. Nothing moved: the pages are untouched and the diary is still there.
Still, something is broken: what was meant to stay secret is no longer secret. In cybersecurity, this is called losing confidentiality.

decouverte.titre: It is like the diary's padlock
decouverte.comme: The padlock does not stop the diary from existing. It decides who has the right to read it.
decouverte.enVrai: Confidentiality means deciding who has the right to see some information, and stopping everyone else from getting to it. For a company, the diary is its data: customer files, passwords, secret plans.

decouverte.question: A burglar photographs your diary without moving anything. What is broken?
options: Access: you can no longer open your diary
decouverte.explanation: The text is untouched and you can still open it. But someone saw what they should not have seen. The other two answers are tempting: they are two other pillars of security, which you will see in the next planets.

decouverte.titre: An email sent to the wrong person
decouverte.texte: An employee wants to send the list of salaries to human resources. She clicks the wrong name and everyone receives it. No hacker, no damaged file. Still, confidentiality is lost. A single mistake is enough.

decouverte.comme: At school, the supervisor has the key to the teachers' room, but not the key to the principal's office. Everyone has only the keys they need.
decouverte.enVrai: This is the principle of least privilege: each person gets just the access they need for their job. The fewer keys there are, the smaller the risk of a leak.

cards.question: Official definition: “confidentiality”
cards.answer: Confidentiality is the concept of limiting access to data to authorized users and systems and restricting access from unauthorized parties.
cards.explanation: Read it again thinking of the padlock: only the right readers have the key.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. You will need to know it word for word: the next cards help you memorize it step by step.

cards.question: Confidentiality is the concept of [[limiting]] access to data to authorized users and systems and restricting access from [[unauthorized]] parties.
cards.answer: Confidentiality is the concept of limiting access to data to authorized users and systems and restricting access from unauthorized parties.
cards.explanation: Two ideas: limit access to authorized people, and block those who are not.

cards.question: Confidentiality is the concept of [[limiting access to data]] to [[authorized users and systems]] and [[restricting access from unauthorized parties]].
cards.answer: Confidentiality is the concept of limiting access to data to authorized users and systems and restricting access from unauthorized parties.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: limit access to data, for authorized users and systems, and block the others.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “confidentiality” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: Confidentiality is the concept of limiting access to data to authorized users and systems and restricting access from unauthorized parties.
cards.explanation: No need to be perfect on the first try: compare, spot the missing word, try again tomorrow.

cards.question: Official definition: “least privilege”
cards.answer: Under least privilege, users are only given enough access to do their jobs — no more and no less.
cards.explanation: Think of the school keys: everyone has only the ones they need.
cards.explanation_more: The manual links it to confidentiality: access to information is given only according to the need-to-know.

cards.question: Under least privilege, users are only given [[enough]] access to do their jobs — no more and [[no less]].
cards.answer: Under least privilege, users are only given enough access to do their jobs — no more and no less.
cards.explanation: Not too much (risk of a leak), not too little (the work cannot be done).

cards.question: Under [[least privilege]], users are only given [[enough access]] to [[do their jobs]] — no more and no less.
cards.answer: Under least privilege, users are only given enough access to do their jobs — no more and no less.
cards.explanation: The name of the principle, the amount of access, and the reason: the job to do.

cards.question: Write the manual's sentence about “least privilege” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: Under least privilege, users are only given enough access to do their jobs — no more and no less.
cards.explanation: Spot the three ideas: only, enough access, no more and no less.

cards.question: Official definition: “PII”
cards.answer: Information that can be used to uniquely identify a person, such as names, birthdates, and Social Security numbers, are considered personally identifiable information (PII), which is usually required by law to be kept highly confidential.
cards.explanation: PII means anything that lets you recognize one specific person.
cards.explanation_more: In English: personally identifiable information. The book adds that the law usually requires keeping it highly confidential.

cards.question: Information that can be used to [[uniquely identify a person]], such as names, birthdates, and Social Security numbers, are considered [[personally identifiable information]] (PII), which is usually required by law to be kept [[highly confidential]].
cards.answer: Information that can be used to uniquely identify a person, such as names, birthdates, and Social Security numbers, are considered personally identifiable information (PII), which is usually required by law to be kept highly confidential.
cards.explanation: The idea: identify someone, the official name (PII), and the duty of secrecy.

cards.question: An employee sends the customer list to the wrong person by mistake. Which pillar is hit?
cards.answer: Confidentiality
cards.explanation: Nobody changed the list: it was only seen by someone who had no right to.

cards.question: Which of these cases makes you lose confidentiality, with no hacker at all?
options: A screen with sensitive data that strangers can see
A power cut that shuts down the server
A typo that changes a number in a database
A hard drive that breaks down
options_why: Here, authorized people can no longer reach the data: that is availability.
Here, a piece of data became wrong: that is integrity.
Here, the data can no longer be reached: that is availability.
cards.answer: A screen with sensitive data that strangers can see
cards.explanation: People who are not authorized can see the information: this is exactly what confidentiality must prevent.
cards.explanation_more: The manual also lists these human mistakes: not encrypting sensitive data and sending an email to the wrong address.

cards.question: Which box does each situation go in?
cards.answer: Confidentiality: the misdirected email and the visible screen. Integrity: the line changed by mistake and the virus. Availability: the website that is down and the ransomware.
cards.explanation: Ask yourself: did someone see what they should not (confidentiality), change something (integrity), or block access (availability)?

items.text: A confidential email goes to the wrong person
A stranger reads a sensitive screen over your shoulder
Someone changes a line in a configuration file by mistake
A virus changes some data
The shop's website is down all Saturday
A ransomware locks all the files

cards.question: Why don't we give every employee access to all the company's files?
cards.answer: The more people can reach some information, the more likely it is to leak, by mistake or on purpose. We give only the access the job needs: this is least privilege.
cards.explanation: Every extra access is an open door for nothing.

cards.question: Name three measures that help protect confidentiality.
cards.answer: Encryption, multifactor authentication (a second check on top of the password) and access based on each person's role. Staff training also helps, because many leaks come from mistakes.
cards.explanation: The first three protect access; training reduces human error.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Confidentiality”: encryption, multifactor authentication and role-based access controls.

cards.question: What is the difference between privacy and confidentiality?
cards.answer: Confidentiality protects all sensitive data. Privacy is the related field that deals only with the confidentiality of personal data.
cards.explanation: Privacy is a special case: the one where the data is about people.

paragraphes: You find your diary. The padlock is closed and nothing is missing. But as you read, you see that some sentences have changed.
Someone scribbled on your pages, then closed the padlock again. Nobody stole anything, and the diary still opens.
Still, you can no longer trust it: you do not know which sentences are yours. In cybersecurity, this is called losing integrity.

decouverte.titre: It is like a diary written in ink
decouverte.comme: Imagine your diary written in ink. If someone crosses out or adds a word, you see it right away. And if you keep a photocopy, you can find the right version again.
decouverte.enVrai: Integrity means keeping data accurate, complete and reliable. Only an authorized person can change it. If someone changes it anyway, we must be able to spot it easily. The photocopy is like a backup.

decouverte.question: An administrator (the person who manages the company's computers) picks the wrong line and changes the wrong setting. No hacker. Is integrity hit?
options: No: without a hacker, it is not an attack
Yes: a piece of data was changed by mistake
decouverte.answer: Yes: a piece of data was changed by mistake
decouverte.explanation: Integrity can also be lost by mistake or by forgetting, not only by attack. Believing that only an attack counts is a common mistake.

decouverte.titre: It is like your parents' signature
decouverte.comme: Your parents sign your school planner. The signature proves it was really them. And they can no longer say “I saw nothing”.
decouverte.enVrai: The digital signature plays this role. It proves who wrote the document: this is authenticity. It also stops people from denying it: this is nonrepudiation. The image stops there: a handwritten signature is easier to fake.

decouverte.texte: You download a game. The site also gives a hash: a short summary of the file, like a fingerprint. Your computer calculates it again after the download. If it is different, the file changed on the way. Do not install it.

cards.question: Official definition: “integrity”
cards.answer: Integrity is the concept of maintaining the accuracy, validity, and completeness of data and systems.
cards.explanation: Think of the diary in ink: nothing is changed or forgotten.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”. You need to know it word for word.

cards.question: Integrity is the concept of maintaining the [[accuracy]], validity, and [[completeness]] of data and systems.
cards.answer: Integrity is the concept of maintaining the accuracy, validity, and completeness of data and systems.
cards.explanation: Three qualities: accuracy (correct), validity (valid), completeness (nothing missing).

cards.question: Integrity is the concept of [[maintaining the accuracy]], [[validity]], and [[completeness of data and systems]].
cards.answer: Integrity is the concept of maintaining the accuracy, validity, and completeness of data and systems.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: keeping accuracy, validity, and the completeness of data and systems.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “integrity” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: Integrity is the concept of maintaining the accuracy, validity, and completeness of data and systems.
cards.explanation: Compare: do you have the three qualities, accuracy, validity and completeness?

cards.question: Official definition: what integrity ensures (“It ensures that data is not manipulated…”)
cards.answer: It ensures that data is not manipulated by anyone other than an authorized party with an authorized purpose, and that any unauthorized manipulation is easily identifiable as such.
cards.explanation: Two protections: only authorized people change the data, and any improper change can be seen.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”: this is the sentence that follows the definition of integrity.

cards.question: It ensures that data is [[not manipulated]] by anyone other than [[an authorized party with an authorized purpose]], and that any [[unauthorized manipulation]] is easily identifiable as such.
cards.answer: It ensures that data is not manipulated by anyone other than an authorized party with an authorized purpose, and that any unauthorized manipulation is easily identifiable as such.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: no manipulation, only by an authorized person, and an improper change must be visible.

cards.question: Official definition: “authenticity”
cards.answer: Authenticity refers to ensuring that data is genuine and that all parties are who they say they are.
cards.explanation: Two truths to check: the document is real, and the people are who they say they are.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. Authenticity is a notion close to integrity.

cards.question: Authenticity refers to ensuring that data is [[genuine]] and that all [[parties]] are who they say they are.
cards.answer: Authenticity refers to ensuring that data is genuine and that all parties are who they say they are.
cards.explanation: Genuine means real, authentic. Parties means the people or systems involved.

cards.question: Authenticity refers to ensuring that [[data is genuine]] and that [[all parties]] are [[who they say they are]].
cards.answer: Authenticity refers to ensuring that data is genuine and that all parties are who they say they are.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: genuine data, all the parties, and they really are who they claim.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “authenticity” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: Authenticity refers to ensuring that data is genuine and that all parties are who they say they are.
cards.explanation: Spot the two halves of the sentence: the data, then the people.

cards.question: Official definition: “nonrepudiation”
cards.answer: Nonrepudiation is a legal principle that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that no party is able to deny their actions (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).
cards.explanation: Think of the signed planner: you can no longer say “it was not me”.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. To repudiate means to deny.

cards.question: Nonrepudiation is a [[legal]] principle that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that no party is able to [[deny]] their actions (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).
cards.answer: Nonrepudiation is a legal principle that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that no party is able to deny their actions (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).
cards.explanation: Two key words: legal (it is first a principle of law) and deny.

cards.question: Nonrepudiation is a [[legal principle]] that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that [[no party is able]] to [[deny their actions]] (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).
cards.answer: Nonrepudiation is a legal principle that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that no party is able to deny their actions (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).
cards.explanation: Three blocks: a legal principle, no party is able to, deny their actions.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “nonrepudiation” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: Nonrepudiation is a legal principle that has a strong parallel in the information security world; this concept requires ensuring that no party is able to deny their actions (e.g., creating, modifying, or deleting data).
cards.explanation: Do not forget the three actions in brackets: creating, modifying, deleting.

cards.question: Official definition: “digital signatures”
cards.answer: Digital signatures are the most common mechanisms used to establish authenticity and nonrepudiation in information systems.
cards.explanation: One digital signature gives two proofs: who signed, and that they cannot deny it.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Integrity”.

cards.question: Digital signatures are the [[most common mechanisms]] used to establish [[authenticity and nonrepudiation]] in [[information systems]].
cards.answer: Digital signatures are the most common mechanisms used to establish authenticity and nonrepudiation in information systems.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the most common mechanisms, the two proofs obtained, and the setting of information systems.

cards.question: A customer says “I never placed this order”, but they signed it. Which idea does the digital signature protect?
cards.answer: Nonrepudiation
cards.explanation: Authenticity proves who wrote it. Nonrepudiation then stops them from denying it.

cards.question: A bank employee types 1000 instead of 100 on a transfer. Nobody meant it. What happens for security?
options: No loss: without an attack, there is no problem
We lose integrity: a piece of data became wrong
We lose confidentiality: someone saw the amount
We lose availability: the transfer is blocked
options_why: Integrity can also be lost by a plain mistake, with no hacker at all.
Nobody read anything without the right to: the data just changed.
The transfer goes through: it is its amount that is wrong.
cards.answer: We lose integrity: a piece of data became wrong
cards.explanation: A correct piece of data became wrong, even with no bad intention.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: integrity can be hit by malicious acts, human error, forgetting or carelessness.

cards.question: Authenticity or nonrepudiation? Sort each situation.
cards.answer: Authenticity: checking the sender and checking that the file is not a fake. Nonrepudiation: stopping a customer from denying an order and keeping the proof of a deletion.
cards.explanation: Authenticity: is it real, is it really them? Nonrepudiation: can they deny it later?

items.text: Check that the message really comes from the person it claims
Check that the file received is not a fake
Stop a customer from saying “I never placed this order”
Keep the proof that an employee really deleted a file

cards.question: Why is a piece of data that is wrong but well protected still dangerous?
cards.answer: People make decisions with this data. If it is wrong, they can make bad choices or take dangerous actions.
cards.explanation: Integrity lets you trust what you read.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: without integrity, staff can make bad decisions, because the information is incorrect.

cards.question: What is the main goal of integrity?
cards.answer: That data stays intact, correct and reliable.
cards.explanation: Three words to remember: intact, correct, reliable.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: “all data remains intact, correct, and reliable”.

cards.question: What if someone changes a file, but we spot it right away and put back the right version?
cards.answer: Integrity was attacked, but it is restored. What matters is to spot the change easily and go back to a healthy state.
cards.explanation: Protecting integrity also means knowing how to repair quickly.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: restoring altered data to a known-good state.

cards.question: [[Digital signatures|signatures]] are used to establish authenticity and nonrepudiation.
cards.answer: Digital signatures are used to establish authenticity and nonrepudiation.
cards.explanation: A signature proves who wrote it and stops them from denying it.

cards.question: Name two measures that help protect integrity.
cards.answer: For example: backups and strict access control. Also: tracking the versions of a file, to go back, and cryptographic hashes.
cards.explanation: They stop an unauthorized change, or let you go back to a healthy version.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: backups, version control, strict access control and cryptographic hashes. Security training helps against accidental mistakes.

paragraphes: Your diary is intact: nobody read it, nobody scribbled in it. But you lost the key to the padlock.
Tonight, you need it, and you cannot open it. It is perfectly protected, but it is no use to you.
In cybersecurity, this is called losing availability.

decouverte.titre: It is like a cash machine
decouverte.comme: A cash machine can be perfectly safe. If it is broken on Saturday night, it is no use to anyone.
decouverte.enVrai: Availability means making sure authorized people can reach the data when they need it. A long breakdown can make a company lose customers and money. The image stops there: a cash machine breaks down by itself, while an attack can also cause the breakdown.

decouverte.question: A file is on the company's shared drive. The drive works and the file is intact. You try to open it: “access denied”. Is the file available?
options: No: if you cannot open it, it no longer exists
Yes, it is available, but it is not accessible to you
decouverte.answer: Yes, it is available, but it is not accessible to you
decouverte.explanation: The file exists and the drive works: it is available. But you do not have permission: it is not accessible. These two words are close, but different.

decouverte.comme: Your teacher posts homework online. If you are not allowed to open the folder, you cannot get to it. If it opens as read-only, you cannot write your answer. If it opens after the deadline, it is too late.
decouverte.enVrai: These are three ideas close to availability. Accessibility: being able to get to it. Usability: being able to do what you need. Timeliness: having it within an acceptable time.

decouverte.texte: A company stores its files with a cloud provider. A contract sets in writing what the provider promises. For example: a service that works almost all the time and answers fast. This contract is called a service level agreement (SLA).

cards.question: Official definition: “availability”
cards.answer: Availability is the concept focused on ensuring that authorized users can access data when they need it.
cards.explanation: Think of the diary key: you must be able to open it at the right time.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”. You need to know it word for word.

cards.question: Availability is the concept focused on ensuring that [[authorized]] users can access data when they [[need]] it.
cards.answer: Availability is the concept focused on ensuring that authorized users can access data when they need it.
cards.explanation: Two key words: authorized (the right people) and need (at the moment of need).

cards.question: Availability is the concept focused on [[ensuring that authorized users]] can [[access data]] [[when they need it]].
cards.answer: Availability is the concept focused on ensuring that authorized users can access data when they need it.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the authorized users, accessing data, when they need it.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “availability” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: Availability is the concept focused on ensuring that authorized users can access data when they need it.
cards.explanation: Compare: did you think of authorized and of when they need it?

cards.question: Official definition: availability in a company (“In enterprise environments…”)
cards.answer: In enterprise environments, the concept of availability entails providing assurance that legitimate parties have timely and uninterrupted access to the systems and data that they need to do their jobs.
cards.explanation: In a company, two words are added: timely (on time) and uninterrupted (no break).
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: In enterprise environments, the concept of availability entails providing [[assurance that legitimate parties]] have [[timely and uninterrupted access]] to the [[systems and data]] that they need to do their jobs.
cards.answer: In enterprise environments, the concept of availability entails providing assurance that legitimate parties have timely and uninterrupted access to the systems and data that they need to do their jobs.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the assurance for legitimate parties, fast and continuous access, the systems and data.

cards.question: Official definition: “accessibility”
cards.answer: Accessibility refers to the ability and ease of a user to use a resource or access data when needed.
cards.explanation: Accessibility means being able to get in: no barrier for authorized people.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”: the manual gives the example of a file moved into a protected folder.

cards.question: Accessibility refers to the [[ability and ease]] of a user to [[use a resource]] or [[access data when needed]].
cards.answer: Accessibility refers to the ability and ease of a user to use a resource or access data when needed.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: ability and ease, using a resource, accessing data when needed.

cards.question: Official definition: “usability”
cards.answer: Usability refers to the ability of a user to meet their needs with available data.
cards.explanation: Usability means being able to use it: a read-only file is available but hard to use.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”: example of a read-only document.

cards.question: Usability refers to the [[ability of a user]] to [[meet their needs]] with [[available data]].
cards.answer: Usability refers to the ability of a user to meet their needs with available data.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the user's ability, meeting their needs, with available data.

cards.question: Official definition: “timeliness”
cards.answer: Timeliness refers to the time expectation for availability of information and resources and is the measure of the time between when information is expected and when it is available for use.
cards.explanation: Timeliness is the waiting time: between when you expect it and when you get it.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”: this delay is set in a service level agreement (SLA).

cards.question: Timeliness refers to the [[time expectation]] for availability of information and resources and is the [[measure of the time]] between when information is [[expected and when it is available]] for use.
cards.answer: Timeliness refers to the time expectation for availability of information and resources and is the measure of the time between when information is expected and when it is available for use.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the expected delay, the measure of time, between expecting it and having it available.

cards.question: The file exists, but you do not have permission to open it. What can we say?
cards.answer: Available, but not accessible
cards.explanation: The file exists and the drive works: it is available. Without permission, it is not accessible.

cards.question: On sale day, a shop's website answers, but takes five minutes to show each page. Which notion is mostly hit?
options_why: Customers can enter the site: nothing stops them.
Customers can shop, but far too slowly.
Nobody read data in secret.
cards.answer: Timeliness
cards.explanation: The site works, but the information arrives too late compared with what people expect.

cards.question: Is this threat to availability malicious or not?
cards.answer: Malicious: denial of service, ransomware, deliberate deletion of files. Not malicious: disk failure, software error, power cut, flood, excessive heat.
cards.explanation: Ask yourself: did someone do it on purpose to cause harm?

items.text: A denial of service (DoS) attack
A ransomware locks the files
A malicious employee deletes files
A hard drive breaks down
A mistake in some software
A power cut
A flood in the server room
Excessive heat in the machine room

cards.question: Why must a company protect itself from natural failures, not only from hackers?
cards.answer: A flood or a power cut blocks access as much as an attack. The result is the same: people can no longer work.
cards.explanation: Availability can be lost through human or natural causes.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: you must plan for human and natural threats, malicious or not.

cards.question: Name two measures that help keep availability.
cards.answer: For example: data backups and redundant storage (copies on several disks). Also: backup power and WAFs (firewalls that protect websites).
cards.explanation: They let you keep working even when something breaks down.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: backups, redundant storage, backup power and web application firewalls (WAF). The cloud adds redundancy.

cards.question: The acceptable delay of a cloud service is written in the [[service level agreement|SLA]].
cards.answer: The acceptable delay of a cloud service is written in the service level agreement.
cards.explanation: SLA stands for service level agreement: it is the contract of the provider's promises.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Availability”.

cards.question: What if some data is perfectly protected by a password, but everyone forgot it?
cards.answer: The data keeps its confidentiality, but availability is lost: authorized people can no longer reach it.
cards.explanation: A protection that is too strong, with no access for the right people, breaks another pillar.

cards.question: You open a document, but only as read-only: you cannot change it. Which notion is missing?
cards.answer: Usability
cards.explanation: The document is available and arrives on time, but you cannot do what you need.

paragraphes: In 1989, the internet is very young. Few people use it, mostly researchers.
A group of experts, the Internet Activities Board (IAB), asks how to behave well in this new place.
It publishes a short text of rules: RFC 1087, titled “Ethics and the Internet”. An RFC is a public document that describes a rule or an idea about the internet.

decouverte.titre: It is like the rules of the swimming pool
decouverte.comme: At the pool, nobody tells you everything. But there are common-sense rules: do not bother the swimmers, do not waste water.
decouverte.enVrai: The 1989 text does the same for the internet. It lists five unacceptable acts done on purpose. Getting in without the right. Disrupting use. Wasting resources. Destroying the integrity of information. Violating privacy. The image stops there: the internet has no lifeguard.

decouverte.question: You deliberately run a program that wastes the capacity of your school's network. You steal nothing. Is it against ethics according to RFC 1087?
decouverte.explanation: The text mentions wasting resources: people, capacity and computers. Stealing is not the only fault.

decouverte.texte: The manual notes that this 1989 text already fits the CIA Triad and privacy. For example, getting in without the right threatens confidentiality. Destroying the integrity of information is about integrity. Disrupting the use of the internet hits availability.

cards.question: Official definition: RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 1 (access, “seeks to…”)
cards.answer: seeks to gain unauthorized access to the resources of the Internet
cards.explanation: The text targets any activity done on purpose (purposely) that seeks to get in without the right.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”. The opening sentence is: “RFC 1087 characterizes as unethical and unacceptable any activity that purposely”.

cards.question: [[seeks to gain]] [[unauthorized access]] to the [[resources of the Internet]]
cards.answer: seeks to gain unauthorized access to the resources of the Internet
cards.explanation: Activity no. 1: unauthorized access to the resources of the internet.

cards.question: Official definition: RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 2 (use, “disrupts…”)
cards.answer: disrupts the intended use of the Internet
cards.explanation: Think of someone who blocks a service that others want to use.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: [[disrupts]] the [[intended use]] of the [[Internet]]
cards.answer: disrupts the intended use of the Internet
cards.explanation: Activity no. 2: disrupting the intended use of the internet.

cards.question: Official definition: RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 3 (waste, “wastes…”)
cards.answer: wastes resources (people, capacity, computer) through such actions
cards.explanation: The three resources in brackets: people, capacity, computers.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: [[wastes resources]] ([[people, capacity, computer]]) through [[such actions]]
cards.answer: wastes resources (people, capacity, computer) through such actions
cards.explanation: Activity no. 3: wasting resources, meaning people, capacity and computers.

cards.question: Official definition: RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 4 (integrity, “destroys…”)
cards.answer: destroys the integrity of computer-based information
cards.explanation: Here we find the integrity of the CIA Triad.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: [[destroys]] the [[integrity]] of [[computer-based information]]
cards.answer: destroys the integrity of computer-based information
cards.explanation: Activity no. 4: destroying the integrity of information stored on computers.

cards.question: Official definition: RFC 1087, unacceptable activity no. 5 (privacy, “compromises…”)
cards.answer: compromises the privacy of users
cards.explanation: It is the shortest of the five: compromising the privacy of users.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: [[compromises]] the [[privacy]] of [[users]]
cards.answer: compromises the privacy of users
cards.explanation: Activity no. 5: compromising the privacy of users.

cards.question: When did the Internet Activities Board publish “Ethics and the Internet” (RFC 1087)?
cards.answer: In January 1989.
cards.explanation: It was in the early days of the internet.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Ethics and the Internet”.

cards.question: Who published the memo “Ethics and the Internet” (RFC 1087)?
cards.answer: The Internet Activities Board (IAB)
cards.explanation: (ISC)2 wrote the CISSP code of ethics. The 1989 memo comes from the IAB.

cards.question: A student deliberately takes down the school network: nobody can connect anymore. Which act of RFC 1087 is involved?
options: It compromises the privacy of users
It destroys the integrity of information
It disrupts the intended use of the internet
It seeks to gain unauthorized access
options_why: Nobody looked at personal data: the service is only blocked.
No information was destroyed or changed.
The student did not try to get in somewhere they had no right to.
cards.answer: It disrupts the intended use of the internet
cards.explanation: A service that others want to use is blocked on purpose: this is a disruption of use.

cards.question: Which unacceptable activity of RFC 1087 matches each situation?
cards.answer: Unauthorized access: getting into a school server and guessing a password. Privacy: sharing private messages or personal data. Integrity: damaging or faking data. Use: taking down or blocking a service.
cards.explanation: Ask yourself what is hit: the entry, people's secrets, accuracy, or the service.

items.text: Get into a school's server without permission
Guess a classmate's password to open their account
Share a classmate's private messages
Show strangers the personal data of users
Deliberately damage another person's data
Deliberately fake a shared file
Deliberately take down a website so nobody can use it
Deliberately stop a service from working normally

cards.question: Why is a text from 1989 still useful to a professional today?
cards.answer: Its rules aim at principles that do not change: access, integrity, use and privacy. They still fit the CIA Triad.
cards.explanation: Tools change, but the principles stay the same.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: the memo is old by the standards of technology, but its principles are still relevant.

cards.question: RFC 1087 is about ethics on the [[internet]] and dates from [[1989]].
cards.answer: RFC 1087 is about ethics on the internet and dates from 1989.
cards.explanation: A text from the very early days of the internet, still relevant today.

cards.question: What if someone wastes resources by mistake, without meaning to? Does RFC 1087 call it unacceptable?
cards.answer: The key word is “purposely”: the text targets acts done on purpose. A mistake is still a security problem, but it is not what the RFC describes.
cards.explanation: RFC 1087 talks about acts done on purpose, not accidents.

cards.question: According to RFC 1087, an activity is unacceptable if it wastes what?
cards.answer: Resources: people, capacity and computers.
cards.explanation: Three resources: people, capacity, computer.

concepts.name: The limits of the triad (NIST, privacy)

paragraphes: You get a message from your best friend: “Send me your password, quick!”.
The message arrived on time, intact, and nobody else read it. Still, your friend did not write it.
The three pillars of the triad do not see this problem. This is one of its limits, which experts tried to fix.

decouverte.question: A secret message, intact and on time, comes from a fake friend. Which idea is missing from the CIA Triad?
options: Authenticity: knowing who the real author is
decouverte.answer: Authenticity: knowing who the real author is
decouverte.explanation: The manual says the triad does not directly deal with authenticity or nonrepudiation. The other two pillars were respected here.

decouverte.titre: It is like a game with three rules
decouverte.comme: A game has three simple rules. The more players and new situations there are, the more unplanned cases appear. Then rules are added.
decouverte.enVrai: The triad is simple, and that is its strength. It dates from the mid-1960s. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) is an American standards organization. It added two ideas in a document called SP 800-33.

decouverte.titre: It is like the attendance register
decouverte.comme: At school, the attendance register shows who is present. If a register goes missing, we can trace it back to the person who took it.
decouverte.enVrai: This is accountability: the actions of a person or a system can be traced to them alone. Without it, there is no way to know who did what.

decouverte.titre: It is like testing the fire alarm
decouverte.comme: A fire alarm is tested every month. Not to set it off, but to be sure it will work on the day there is smoke.
decouverte.enVrai: This is assurance: confidence that the protections really work as planned. A company must not only install protections, it must be able to rely on them.

decouverte.texte: You have private photos on your phone. Only you decide who can see them and share them. This is the idea of privacy. For a company, it is the data of its customers and employees. Privacy is close to confidentiality, but it only covers data about people.

cards.question: Official definition: “accountability” (NIST)
cards.answer: accountability (that actions of an entity may be traced uniquely to that entity)
cards.explanation: Think of the attendance register: one action, one person responsible.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”: NIST SP 800-33 adds accountability and assurance to the triad.

cards.question: accountability (that [[actions]] of an entity may be [[traced]] uniquely to that entity)
cards.answer: accountability (that actions of an entity may be traced uniquely to that entity)
cards.explanation: Two key words: actions (what you do) and traced (you can go back to the author).

cards.question: accountability (that [[actions of an entity]] may be [[traced uniquely]] to [[that entity]])
cards.answer: accountability (that actions of an entity may be traced uniquely to that entity)
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the actions of an entity, traced uniquely, to that same entity.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “accountability” according to NIST from memory (in English).
cards.answer: accountability (that actions of an entity may be traced uniquely to that entity)
cards.explanation: Check the word uniquely: one action must lead to only one entity.

cards.question: Official definition: “assurance” (NIST)
cards.answer: assurance (the basis for confidence that the security measures, both technical and operational, work as intended to protect the system and the information it processes)
cards.explanation: Think of the alarm test: confidence that the protections really work.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”. Technical means the tools; operational means the way they are used.

cards.question: assurance (the basis for [[confidence]] that the security measures, both technical and [[operational]], work as intended to protect the system and the information it processes)
cards.answer: assurance (the basis for confidence that the security measures, both technical and operational, work as intended to protect the system and the information it processes)
cards.explanation: Two key words: confidence (trust) and operational (the way the measures are used).

cards.question: assurance (the [[basis for confidence]] that the [[security measures]], both technical and operational, [[work as intended]] to protect the system and the information it processes)
cards.answer: assurance (the basis for confidence that the security measures, both technical and operational, work as intended to protect the system and the information it processes)
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the basis for confidence, the security measures, they work as intended.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “assurance” according to NIST from memory (in English).
cards.answer: assurance (the basis for confidence that the security measures, both technical and operational, work as intended to protect the system and the information it processes)
cards.explanation: Split it in three: the confidence, the technical and operational measures, protecting the system and the information.

cards.question: Official definition: “privacy”
cards.answer: Privacy, as defined in the (ISC)2 glossary, is the right of human individuals to control the distribution of information about themselves.
cards.explanation: Think of your photos: you decide who sees them.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”. Privacy is often handled outside the security team, but it is close to confidentiality.

cards.question: Privacy, as defined in the (ISC)2 glossary, is the [[right]] of human individuals to control the [[distribution]] of information about themselves.
cards.answer: Privacy, as defined in the (ISC)2 glossary, is the right of human individuals to control the distribution of information about themselves.
cards.explanation: Two key words: right (a right) and distribution (sharing).

cards.question: Privacy, as defined in the (ISC)2 glossary, is the [[right of human individuals]] to [[control the distribution]] of [[information about themselves]].
cards.answer: Privacy, as defined in the (ISC)2 glossary, is the right of human individuals to control the distribution of information about themselves.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the right of individuals, controlling the distribution, information about themselves.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “privacy” from memory (in English).
cards.answer: Privacy, as defined in the (ISC)2 glossary, is the right of human individuals to control the distribution of information about themselves.
cards.explanation: Do not forget the start: as defined in the (ISC)2 glossary.

cards.question: We can find out which employee deleted a file. Which idea is this?
cards.answer: Accountability
cards.explanation: The action is tied to one person: accountability. Assurance is the confidence that the protections work.

cards.question: NIST SP 800-33 takes the CIA Triad as three of its five goals. What are the other two?
options_why: These two ideas are mentioned as limits of the triad, but they are not the two additions of NIST.
These notions come from Parker's hexad, not from NIST.
These are protection measures, not security goals.
cards.answer: Accountability and assurance
cards.explanation: NIST kept the three pillars and added accountability and assurance.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad” (NIST Special Publication 800-33).

cards.question: Is this idea in the CIA Triad, or added by NIST?
cards.answer: In the CIA Triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability. Added by NIST: accountability and assurance.
cards.explanation: NIST keeps the three pillars and adds two ideas to reach five goals.

items.text: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Accountability
Assurance

cards.question: Why is the CIA Triad no longer enough on its own?
cards.answer: It is very simple and dates from the 1960s. With systems spread over many computers and new technologies, it does not directly deal with authenticity or nonrepudiation.
cards.explanation: Its simplicity is its strength, but also its limit.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”: the triad comes from theoretical work from the mid-1960s.

cards.question: A company regularly tests its protections to be sure they work. Which NIST idea does this show?
options_why: Accountability links an action to its author, it does not check the protections.
Privacy is about data on people, not about whether the protections work.
cards.answer: Assurance
cards.explanation: Testing gives a basis of confidence that the measures work as planned.

cards.question: What is NIST?
cards.answer: The National Institute of Standards and Technology: an American standards organization. Its work is still a reference for good security practices.
cards.explanation: Remember the acronym: NIST, and its role as a reference.
cards.explanation_more: The manual says NIST's work is still influential in setting down good security practices for systems. That it is an American organization is outside the manual.

cards.question: NIST adds [[accountability]] and [[assurance]] to the triad.
cards.answer: NIST adds accountability and assurance to the triad.
cards.explanation: Two additions: actions traced to their author, and confidence in the protections.

cards.question: What if a company could not tell who changed a file?
cards.answer: It would lose accountability: it could not link the action to its author. It could neither fix the mistake nor spot an abuse.
cards.explanation: Knowing who did what is the basis for fixing and preventing.

cards.question: What is the title of the NIST document (SP 800-33) that takes up the CIA Triad?
cards.answer: Underlying Technical Models for Information Technology Security.
cards.explanation: A title to recognize, with the number 800-33.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”.

paragraphes: Your friend loses their USB stick on the bus. It holds their homework, but the homework is encrypted: nobody can read it. The homework is intact.
Still, someone else now has the stick in their pocket. Your friend has lost control of where their information is.
A pioneer of security, Donn B. Parker, added new ideas to the triad to cover this kind of case.

decouverte.titre: It is like a die with six faces
decouverte.comme: A die has six clearly separate faces. None is a copy of another, and each has its own number.
decouverte.enVrai: Parker's hexad (Parkerian Hexad) has six ideas: the three pillars of the triad, plus three others. Parker wanted them to be atomic (impossible to split further) and nonoverlapping (each one is different from the others).

decouverte.question: You lose an encrypted, virus-free USB stick on the bus. Which of Parker's ideas is hit the most?
decouverte.explanation: The data is neither read nor changed, but you no longer know where the stick is. The other two ideas are tempting, but they are about something else.

decouverte.titre: It is like a recipe in an unknown language
decouverte.comme: You have a cake recipe, intact and complete. But it is written in a language you do not understand. You have it, and yet it is no use to you.
decouverte.enVrai: This is utility: is the information useful to the person who gets it? Information can be available and still unusable.

decouverte.texte: An email arrives in your director's name. Authenticity asks: who really wrote it? A file is encrypted and its key is lost: utility is lost. A USB stick is stolen: possession or control is lost.

cards.question: Official definition: Parkerian Hexad, “Confidentiality”
cards.answer: Confidentiality: The limits on who has access to information
cards.explanation: The same pillar as in the triad, said differently: who has the right to get to it.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”: the first of the six ideas of Parker's hexad.

cards.question: Confidentiality: The [[limits]] on [[who has access]] to [[information]]
cards.answer: Confidentiality: The limits on who has access to information
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the limits, who has access, to the information.

cards.question: Official definition: Parkerian Hexad, “Integrity”
cards.answer: Integrity: Whether the information is in its intended state
cards.explanation: In the intended state: not damaged, not changed by mistake.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: second idea of the hexad.

cards.question: Integrity: [[Whether]] the [[information]] is in its [[intended state]]
cards.answer: Integrity: Whether the information is in its intended state
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the question Whether, the information, its intended state.

cards.question: Official definition: Parkerian Hexad, “Availability”
cards.answer: Availability: Whether the information can be accessed in a timely manner
cards.explanation: The key word is timely: on time, when you need it.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: third idea of the hexad.

cards.question: Availability: [[Whether the information]] can be [[accessed]] in a [[timely manner]]
cards.answer: Availability: Whether the information can be accessed in a timely manner
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the question, accessing the information, in a timely manner.

cards.question: Official definition: Parkerian Hexad, “Authenticity”
cards.answer: Authenticity: The proper attribution of the person who created the information
cards.explanation: To attribute is to say who the author is: the right person, not an impostor.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: fourth idea of the hexad, the first one added to the triad.

cards.question: Authenticity: The [[proper attribution]] of the [[person who created]] the [[information]]
cards.answer: Authenticity: The proper attribution of the person who created the information
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the proper attribution, the person who created it, the information.

cards.question: Official definition: Parkerian Hexad, “Utility”
cards.answer: Utility: The usefulness of the information
cards.explanation: Think of the recipe in an unknown language: intact, but useless.
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: fifth idea of the hexad.

cards.question: [[Utility]]: The [[usefulness]] of the [[information]]
cards.answer: Utility: The usefulness of the information
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the name, utility, usefulness, and the information.

cards.question: Official definition: Parkerian Hexad, “Possession or control”
cards.answer: Possession or control: The physical state where the information is maintained
cards.explanation: It is the real place where the information is kept: is the USB stick still with you?
cards.explanation_more: Official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: sixth idea of the hexad.

cards.question: Possession or control: The [[physical state]] where the [[information]] is [[maintained]]
cards.answer: Possession or control: The physical state where the information is maintained
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the physical state, the information, where it is kept.

cards.question: An encrypted USB stick is lost on the bus. Which of Parker's ideas is hit the most?
cards.answer: Possession or control
cards.explanation: The information is neither read nor changed, but you no longer control where it is.

cards.question: Parker keeps the CIA Triad and adds three ideas. Which ones?
options_why: These notions come from NIST and from the manual, not from Parker's hexad.
Authenticity is in Parker's hexad, but not nonrepudiation or privacy.
These are protection measures, not ideas of the model.
cards.answer: Authenticity, utility, possession or control
cards.explanation: These three additions, with the triad, make six ideas: this is the hexad.

cards.question: Is this idea already in the CIA Triad, or added by Parker?
cards.answer: Already in the triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability. Added by Parker: authenticity, utility, possession or control.
cards.explanation: You already know the first three. The other three are Parker's new ideas.

items.text: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Authenticity
Utility
Possession or control

cards.question: Why did Parker want ideas that are “atomic” and nonoverlapping?
cards.answer: Atomic: it cannot be split any further. Nonoverlapping: each idea is different from the others. So no idea repeats another.
cards.explanation: Six clearly separate ideas describe risks more clearly.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Limitations of the CIA Triad”: concepts that are “atomic” and “nonoverlapping”.

cards.question: Who proposed the most widespread extension of the CIA Triad?
cards.answer: Donn B. Parker, a pioneer of information security. His model is called the Parkerian Hexad.
cards.explanation: Hexad means a group of six.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. The manual adds that other work produced dozens of information security models.

cards.question: A company loses an encrypted laptop in a taxi. Which idea of the hexad is mostly involved, and why?
cards.answer: Possession or control: the company no longer knows where the information is. Encryption may protect the secret, but physical control is lost.
cards.explanation: The secret can stay protected while control of the object is lost.

cards.question: Parker's hexad adds authenticity, utility and [[possession]] or [[control]] to the triad.
cards.answer: Parker's hexad adds authenticity, utility and possession or control to the triad.
cards.explanation: Three additions, which give with the triad the six ideas of the hexad.

cards.question: A file arrives on time, but you cannot read it. Which of Parker's ideas is hit?
cards.answer: Utility
cards.explanation: It arrives on time: availability is respected. But it is no use to you: utility is missing.
